title: Not Doing the Assignment Isn’t the Same as Not Learning
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey takes aim at the popular argument that having AI do your homework is like sending a friend to the gym to lift weights for you. His counter is a matter of logic: a student who skips an assignment has only failed to do that assignment, which does not prove the student learned nothing. He uses himself as the example, a person who never took the instructor's course and still learned plenty. He then widens the critique to higher education's inflated sense of its own impact, questioning how much a single course of 37.5 hours can change a student. The same reasoning undercuts the claim that group projects are needed because students will work in groups later. His conclusion is a challenge to educators to ask what else students might do in a course that benefits them if traditional assessment no longer captures learning.
points: The gym analogy confuses a student not completing an assignment with a student not learning, and Dempsey argues those are logically distinct claims.
Learning happens through many channels outside any one course, so assuming an assignment is the only route to a goal overstates its importance.
Educators tend to overrate the impact of a single course, which Dempsey illustrates with the arithmetic of 37.5 contact hours over 15 weeks.
The 'students will need this in the workforce' justification for group projects ignores years of group experience in families, sports, dorms and K-12.
If AI weakens traditional assessment, the productive response is to redesign what students do in a course rather than to defend the old assignment.
quotes: I take it the idea is that AI is your friend, the gym is homework or some educational activity, and building muscle is learning. So, if you have AI do your schoolwork for you, you aren’t going to learn anything.
It only follows that I didn’t go to the gym. It of course doesn’t follow that I didn’t do some other activity to build muscle!
Take me, as an example. Actually me. I never took your course. I never completed any of the assignments you believe are somehow essential, or at least helpful, for students.
I mean, honestly, how much immediate and long-term impact do we actually think we can have by spending 37.5 hours, over 15 weeks, at 10 a.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, with some random 18-year-old?

It is quite unclear to me why we think students have never had the opportunity to work with others—to plan, to push through conflict, to achieve something together—outside this course and this project.

If the goal is to support student learning around your discipline and students are not learning it through traditional assessment because they’re just having AI do it for them, then what other things might they do to benefit from their time in your course?
